Litchfield.wildlife_intro:
Wildlife work in Litchfield is country work around historic houses. Bats roost in the attics and barns of colonials around the Green and on the farm roads, squirrels and flying squirrels use old chimneys and eaves, and raccoons split their time between barns, woodpiles, and houses. Around Bantam Lake, beavers and muskrats work the shoreline, while porcupines chew outbuilding wood in the wooded parts of town and fishers pass through the White Memorial woods and other large forest blocks.

The age of the buildings sets the scope: original woodwork, stone foundations, and attached barns give animals routes that a newer house would not, and sealing has to be done in a way that suits a historic home. Lake cottages opened in spring sometimes reveal a winter of squirrel or bat use. Our crew inspects the house and the outbuildings together, removes animals humanely, and seals entries carefully. Fall is our busiest season here, as bats, squirrels, and rodents all look for winter quarters in these older structures.

Squirrels work the mature trees around the Green, woodchucks burrow in the farm fields and under outbuildings, and fishers and porcupines are part of life in the deeper woods.

Jobs often involve more than the house — a barn with bats, a shed with a woodchuck burrow, and a chimney a raccoon has claimed, all on one property. Our crew inspects the full property, removes animals humanely under our CT DEEP NWCO license, and seals structures properly. In summer we plan bat work around the June to mid-August exclusion pause while young bats cannot fly.

Thomaston.wildlife_intro:
Thomaston packs a lot of wildlife into a small town. The Naugatuck River runs past the western neighborhoods, Branch Brook cuts through the center, and woods climb the hills on every side, so raccoons, skunks, and opossums are regular visitors to the compact older streets. Squirrels and bats use the aging rooflines and chimneys of the clock-era housing, woodchucks burrow under sheds on the hillsides, and mice move into stone foundations each fall across town.

Most of our Thomaston jobs are thorough sealing jobs at heart: a squirrel entry at a gable, a gap at the chimney flashing, and a foundation crack the homeowner never saw, all on the same house. Porches and sheds give skunks and woodchucks den sites a few feet from the back door. Our crew removes the animals, screens and seals the structures, and checks the roofline while we are there. Spring denning and fall move-in are the peaks, and small towns like this reward getting the whole house done at once.

Torrington.wildlife_intro:
Torrington is the working city of the Litchfield Hills, and its wildlife calls bridge city and country. Downtown and the older neighborhoods produce raccoons in chimneys, squirrels in multi-family rooflines, rats around older commercial blocks, and bats in pre-war attics. Toward Burrville, Torringford, and the city's wooded edges, the calls shift to woodchucks, skunks, porcupines chewing outbuildings, and the occasional fisher complaint from small farms and chicken keepers along the Naugatuck River branches.

Older Torrington buildings reward a full inspection: stone foundations admit mice and chipmunks, porches shelter skunk dens, and layered roofs hide bat and squirrel entries. Our crew removes animals humanely, seals the structure, and screens porches and sheds in the same visit whenever possible. Winter in the hills is cold, so fall sealing work is heavy here — squirrels, bats, and rodents all compete for the same warm attics, and a house closed up properly in October rarely calls us back in January.

Watertown.wildlife_intro:
Watertown sits above the Naugatuck valley with one foot in the suburbs and one in farm country, and our calls reflect that. Squirrels and bats occupy the attics of Oakville and the center, raccoons work barns and chicken coops on the rural roads, and woodchucks and skunks are standard under sheds and decks throughout town. Steele Brook and the woods of Black Rock State Park thread habitat between neighborhoods, and larger wooded lots mean animals often den on the same property they are raiding.

Because so many Watertown properties have outbuildings, our crew inspects beyond the house: a sealed home with an open barn just moves the raccoons fifty feet. We remove animals humanely, secure the entries, and advise on feed storage and coop repairs that keep fishers and foxes from succeeding. Spring is denning season in chimneys and under porches, summer brings bats and woodchucks, and fall brings the rush to close houses and barns before the Litchfield Hills winter sets in.

Winsted.wildlife_intro:
Winsted's two rivers meet downtown and Highland Lake stretches along its western side, so water shapes the wildlife work here. Bats roost in the mill-era homes along Main Street and in lake cottages, raccoons work the Mad and Still River corridors and the trash routes of the compact neighborhoods, and squirrels are constant in the older rooflines. Around the lake, muskrats and the occasional beaver appear at shorelines, and skunks and woodchucks work the yards climbing the hills.

Many Highland Lake cottages were built for summers and later winterized in stages, which leaves gaps at additions and rooflines that bats and squirrels find easily. Downtown, older multi-family homes share entries the way city buildings do. Our crew inspects the whole structure, removes animals humanely, and seals with care for older materials. Lake homeowners benefit from a check before opening up in spring, and fall sealing keeps squirrels and rodents from spending the long hill-country winter in the attic.
